title: Given a string, find the minimum number of characters you must insert anywhere to make it a palindrome. Explain how the Palindromic Subsequence pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Minimum Insertions to Form a Palindrome (Fewest Additions for Symmetry)

s1_definition.profdef: The Minimum Insertions to Form a Palindrome problem is solved with the Palindromic Subsequence pattern. Every character outside the longest palindromic subsequence lacks a mirror partner and needs one inserted, so the answer is the string length minus the longest palindromic subsequence length. s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Minimum Insertions to Form a Palindrome problem is solved with the Palindromic Subsequence pattern. Every character outside the longest palindromic subsequence lacks a mirror partner and needs one inserted, so the answer is the string length minus the longest palindromic subsequence length. This gives a quadratic time and space dynamic program.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India pads short reference codes into a symmetric canonical shape by adding the fewest characters so the code reads the same both ways. The fewest insertions equal the code length minus its longest symmetric core.

**One line to remember:** Minimum insertions equal the string length minus the longest palindromic subsequence length.

sections.s2_technical:
Think of the characters already in the longest palindromic subsequence as the ones that keep their symmetry for free. Every other character is unmatched, and the only way to make the whole string symmetric without removing anything is to insert a mirror partner for each unmatched character. So the number of insertions equals the number of unmatched characters, which is the string length minus the longest palindromic subsequence length.

We compute the longest palindromic subsequence with the two-ended range table: `for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) { dp[i][i] = 1; for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) dp[i][j] = s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j) ? 2 + dp[i+1][j-1] : Math.max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]); }` and return `n - dp[0][n-1]`. A concrete check: a code of length five whose longest symmetric core is three needs two insertions. Senior nuance: this equals the minimum deletions to make a palindrome, because deleting an unmatched character and inserting its mirror are two symmetric fixes for the same imbalance, and both reduce to the same longest palindromic subsequence quantity.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India pads short reference codes into a symmetric canonical shape so they fit a fixed symmetric template, and it needs the fewest characters to insert into each code to make it read the same both ways without removing anything. Trying all insertion combinations is exponential. This is exactly how the Minimum Insertions to Form a Palindrome works: it computes the longest symmetric core with the Palindromic Subsequence pattern and subtracts it from the length.

The code defines a `CodePaddingService` exposing `minInsertions(code)` returning the minimum insertions. A `Demo` runs it over a sample code and logs the insertion count.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the code ABCDA. We want the fewest insertions that make it a palindrome.

Step 1 — We build the longest palindromic subsequence table. Single characters seed the diagonal with length one.

Step 2 — The ends A and A of the whole code match, so the answer for the full range is two plus the core of the inner range BCD.

Step 3 — Inside BCD all three characters differ pairwise, so its longest palindromic subsequence is one, any single character.

Step 4 — The full range therefore has longest palindromic subsequence two plus one equals three, meaning a symmetric core such as ABA of length three sits inside the five-character code.

Step 5 — The minimum insertions equal five minus three, which is two, since the two unmatched inner characters each need a mirror inserted. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:17:21 PM com.bank.codepad.service.CodePaddingService minInsertions
INFO: Min insertions to make ABCDA a palindrome = 2
Oct 27, 2026 9:17:21 PM com.bank.codepad.CodePaddingApplication main
INFO: Insertions to canonicalise code ABCDA is 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: code = "ABCDA" (length 5)
    │
    ▼
  longest palindromic subsequence table
    │ ends A==A → 2 + core(BCD)
    │ BCD: all differ → core 1
    │ full range → 2 + 1 = 3
    ▼
  answer = length - LPS = 5 - 3 = 2
    ▼
  Output: min insertions = 2
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Minimum Insertions to Form a Palindrome is another direct application of the Palindromic Subsequence pattern. The characters that already belong to the longest palindromic subsequence keep their symmetry for free, and every other character is unmatched. Since I am only allowed to insert, each unmatched character needs a mirror partner inserted on the other side, so the number of insertions equals the number of unmatched characters, which is the string length minus the longest palindromic subsequence length.

I compute the longest palindromic subsequence with the familiar two-ended range table, adding two to the inner answer when the ends match and otherwise dropping one end, and then I subtract that corner value from the length. The whole thing is quadratic in time and space. The connection I emphasise is that this number is identical to the minimum deletions to make the string a palindrome, because deleting an unmatched character and inserting its mirror are two symmetric ways to fix exactly the same imbalance.

At the National Bank of India I used this to pad short reference codes into a symmetric canonical shape that fit a fixed template, where the team needed the fewest characters to insert so the code read the same both ways without deleting anything. I computed the longest symmetric core and subtracted it from the code length. Explaining that the free characters form a palindromic subsequence, that each leftover character needs one inserted mirror, and that this equals the minimum deletions figure is what proves to an interviewer that I understand this facet of the Palindromic Subsequence pattern.
